Final screening also checked the separate, matching-sample journal report c246: Chen et al. (2026), Investigating student engagement with personalised generative AI feedback: Effects on creative problem-solving and feedback uptake, Australasian Journal of Educational Technology 42(4), 165-185, doi:10.14742/ajet.11512 (local PDF: C:/Dropbox/Research/ai-lab/literature/creativity/Chen et al (2026) - Investigating student engagement with personalised generative AI feedback.pdf). source.title_on_document: Effects of Personalized Generative AI on Student Creativity: Evidence from Creative Performance, Self-efficacy, and Attention Allocation

supplement.holds: c041 does not refer to supplementary material, an online appendix, or a data repository; its complete 13-page PDF ends with references. Its statistics are in Sect. 4.1/Fig. 4 and Tables 1-2. The separate related report c246 has an embedded Appendix (PDF pp. 20-21, Tables A1-A2) with tutor settings and prompt/feedback examples, not additional outcome statistics. c246 reports z statistics and confidence intervals for r in its main-text Table 2 (PDF p. 11); these are not a supplement to c041.

paper_design_summary: Sixty-two students (32 undergraduates and 30 graduate students) each completed two Product Improvement Tasks individually in a laboratory, writing three solutions per task with either standard ChatGPT-4 or the personalized GPT-4 tutor Mr. Ranedeer. The chapter describes counterbalanced tool order (31 students per sequence); the matching-sample journal report c246 explicitly shows random assignment of feedback sequence (c041 PDF p. 6, Fig. 2; c246 PDF p. 9, Fig. 3). Two trained raters blind to condition scored the written solutions on quality, elaboration, and originality (1-5), and the conditions were compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; self-efficacy and eye tracking were also measured.

studies.label: Within-subject lab experiment: personalized GPT-4 tutor (Mr. Ranedeer) vs standard ChatGPT-4, Product Improvement Task

assignment.what_was_assigned: The order of standard ChatGPT-4 and personalized Mr. Ranedeer feedback was randomly assigned, with 31 students per sequence, as explicitly shown in c246 Fig. 3 for the matching sample. Every student used both tools, one per task. c041 itself states only that order was counterbalanced; its randomized presentation of solutions to raters is a separate procedure. c246 identifies PIT 1 as the stuffed bunny and PIT 2 as the portable coffee maker; Fig. 3 shows both groups completing PIT 1 then PIT 2, with the AI order reversed between groups (c246 PDF pp. 8-9). The shared-sample inference and its evidence are documented in sample_overlap.
assignment.locator: c246 PDF p. 9 (printed p. 173), Fig. 3, allocation box (visually checked) and N = 31 under each sequence; c041 PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Sect. 3.3 and Fig. 2 describe the matching counterbalanced laboratory experiment. c246 PDF file: C:/Dropbox/Research/ai-lab/literature/creativity/Chen et al (2026) - Investigating student engagement with personalised generative AI feedback.pdf

arms.name: Personalized GAI (Mr. Ranedeer)
arms.description: GPT-4-powered tutor customized via OpenAI's 'Explore GPTs' platform and implemented via prompt engineering. Three stages: students set learning preferences (e.g., feedback tone, cognitive style) and co-designed a learning plan; the tutor asked Socratic-style heuristic questions; then it gave goal-aligned feedback and strategic prompts (e.g., idea refinement, elaboration cues) during solution elaboration (PDF p. 5, Sect. 3.2.1; Fig. 1).

arms.name: Standard GAI (ChatGPT-4)
arms.description: ChatGPT-4 giving generic feedback in two stages: broad suggestions in response to students' queries, then solution generation on further input; open-ended exploration with minimal structure (PDF p. 5, Sect. 3.2.1; Fig. 1).

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions or dropouts are reported in either report. c041 states that each of 62 students completed both tasks (Abstract; Sect. 3.1), and c246 calls 62 the final sample size (PDF p. 5, Participants). Randomized counts come from c246 Fig. 3: 31 assigned to each feedback sequence, for 62 people total; because this is a crossover, the same 62 are counted in each AI arm. c041 Fig. 2 gives 15 undergraduates and 16 graduates in the standard-first sequence and 17 undergraduates and 14 graduates in the personalized-first sequence. The analyzed count is 62 for the study and each AI condition; neither report prints an outcome-specific n beside the creativity tests. The chapter alone does not establish randomization.
participants.who: 32 undergraduates and 30 graduate students (33.9% male), aged 18-27 (M = 22.6, SD = 2.5), from social sciences, life sciences, and technical disciplines; almost all had prior GAI experience, with more familiarity with ChatGPT than with Mr. Ranedeer; compensated.
participants.country: China (c246 PDF pp. 4-5, Participants, for the matching sample; c041 itself does not name the participants' country)
participants.quote: Sixty-two students (32 undergraduates and 30 graduate students; 33.9% male) participated in the study.
participants.locator: c041 PDF p. 4 (printed p. 379), Sect. 3.1; PDF p. 1 (printed p. 376), Abstract; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 381), Fig. 2. Corroborating c246 PDF pp. 4-5 (printed pp. 168-169), Participants, and PDF p. 9 (printed p. 173), Fig. 3, for randomized sequences.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (standard) and Mr. Ranedeer, a custom GPT built on OpenAI's GPT-4 via the 'Explore GPTs' platform (personalized); both used through the OpenAI web interface
ai_tool.how_used: Participants typed prompts to the assigned chatbot in a split screen, with the AI chat on the left and a document workspace on the right (Fig. 3), while writing three product-improvement solutions. Standard arm: ChatGPT-4 gave broad suggestions on request and generated whole solutions on further input. Personalized arm: Mr. Ranedeer first set feedback preferences and a learning plan, then asked Socratic questions, then gave goal-aligned feedback and strategic prompts such as idea refinement and elaboration cues; Fig. 1 shows it also proposing content in that last stage. Both arms are free chat with GPT-4. They differ in the tutor configuration, which the ai_design contrast tests (PDF p. 5, Sect. 3.2.1, Fig. 1; PDF p. 8, Fig. 3).

task.description: Product Improvement Task (Torrance, 1966): propose three solutions, as original and useful as possible, to improve a common product using the assigned AI tool. c041 names a stuffed bunny and a portable coffee machine but does not specify their assignment (PDF pp. 6-7, Sect. 3.4.1). The matching-sample c246 report identifies PIT 1 as the stuffed bunny and PIT 2 as the portable coffee maker; its Fig. 3 shows PIT 1 followed by PIT 2 in both sequences, with standard and personalized AI in opposite orders (c246 PDF pp. 8-9, Procedure and Fig. 3). Thus each product is used with each AI configuration across the two sequence groups. Participants wrote their solutions in a document workspace beside the chat (c041 PDF p. 8, Fig. 3).
task.duration: About 17 min (SD = 7) in the standard condition and 20 min (SD = 6) in the personalized condition; a five-minute break between tasks (PDF p. 6, printed p. 381, Sect. 3.3).

outcomes.name: Creative performance: quality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two trained raters blind to condition rated the solutions on a five-point Likert scale (1 = worst, 5 = best); quality = the extent to which a solution addresses the task objective; solutions were shown to raters in randomized order; Cronbach's alpha = 0.88; final score = mean of the two raters (PDF p. 7, printed p. 382, Sect. 3.4.1). The paper calls the raters trained, not experts. It does not say how the three solutions per task were combined into one score.

contrasts.reported: Personalized M = 3.50, SD = 1.00 vs standard M = 3.08, SD = 1.12; Wilcoxon signed-rank p = .001; r = .42. No Z, SE, or CI printed; no n printed with the result (62 students did both tasks, Abstract and Sect. 3.1).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Sect. 4.1; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 384), Fig. 4A

outcomes.name: Creative performance: elaboration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same two trained raters blind to condition, same five-point scale and procedure; elaboration = the amount of detail provided; Cronbach's alpha = 0.90; mean of the two raters (PDF p. 7, printed p. 382, Sect. 3.4.1).

contrasts.reported: Personalized M = 3.58, SD = 1.17 vs standard M = 2.48, SD = 1.04; Wilcoxon signed-rank p < .001; r = .62. No Z, SE, or CI printed; no n printed with the result.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Sect. 4.1; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 384), Fig. 4A

outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same two trained raters blind to condition, same five-point scale and procedure; originality = the novelty of the idea; Cronbach's alpha = 0.86; mean of the two raters (PDF p. 7, printed p. 382, Sect. 3.4.1).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: c246: Chen et al. (2026), Investigating student engagement with personalised generative AI feedback: Effects on creative problem-solving and feedback uptake, Australasian Journal of Educational Technology 42(4), 165-185, doi:10.14742/ajet.11512. Treat as one shared sample for deduplication, not two independent experiments. This is an inference from source matching: both report 62 students, matching sex composition and rounded age statistics, the same two AI tools and product tasks, 31 students per sequence, identical condition-specific task times and rating-reliability values, and identical means, SDs, and p-values for all three creativity outcomes. Neither report explicitly cross-identifies or cites the other. Use one sample_id and only one primary record per sample, question, and comparison type; retain each report's statistics with its own provenance.

eligibility.reason: All three criteria are met for S1 using c041 and the independently checked matching-sample report c246. Criterion 1: c246 Fig. 3 explicitly labels random assignment of feedback sequence, with 31 students per order (PDF p. 9, printed p. 173); c041 describes the matching laboratory crossover (PDF p. 6, Sect. 3.3/Fig. 2). The linkage is a documentary inference from matching sample details, procedures and identical creativity means, SDs and p-values, documented in sample_overlap. Both conditions provide generative-AI assistance to the participants' own creative work; standard ChatGPT-4 is the comparison configuration, so the contrast is ai_design (c041 PDF p. 5, Sect. 3.2.1). Criterion 2: 62 people were analyzed, with the same people in both AI conditions and no participant exclusions reported (c041 PDF pp. 1 and 4; c246 PDF p. 5, Participants). Criterion 3: two trained raters blind to condition scored written solutions for quality, elaboration and originality while AI was available for their production (c041 PDF pp. 6-7, Sect. 3.4.1). Treat c041 and c246 as one sample for pooling. Remaining aggregation and reporting discrepancies do not change these criteria.

one_line_finding: Among 62 analyzed students, personalized GPT-4 feedback produced higher rated quality (3.50 vs 3.08, p = .001, r = .42) and elaboration (3.58 vs 2.48, p < .001, r = .62) than standard ChatGPT-4, with no significant originality difference (2.92 vs 3.13, p = .098, r = .18), using the values printed in c041 (PDF p. 8, printed p. 383, Sect. 4.1; Fig. 4A).
open_questions: How were the three solutions per task combined into the participant-level creativity score used in the Wilcoxon tests? Both c041 (PDF p. 7, Sect. 3.4.1) and c246 (PDF p. 8, CPS performance) explain averaging the two raters but not aggregating the three solutions. Authors or participant-level scoring data would settle this; it affects extraction and precision, not whether creativity was scored on output or whether 62 people participated.

Why do the reports give different creativity effect sizes despite identical arm means, SDs and p-values? c041 prints quality r = .42, elaboration r = .62 and originality r = .18 (PDF p. 8, Sect. 4.1); c246 prints z = -3.24, -6.25 and -1.65 and r = -0.41, -0.79 and -0.21, respectively (PDF p. 11, Table 2). The journal table identifies the discrepancy but does not explain it or explicitly correct c041. Preserve each report's numbers; obtain the authors' effect-size definitions/calculations or data before resolving the conflict or deriving paired precision. No eligibility criterion depends on which r is correct.

What do the error bars in c041 Fig. 4B represent? The caption says standard deviations, but the plotted self-efficacy bars are much smaller than the SDs of 0.99 and 1.19 printed in Sect. 4.1 (PDF pp. 8-9). They cannot be relabeled as standard errors from the figure alone. Author clarification would settle this; self-efficacy is not an output-scored outcome, so this does not affect eligibility or the three coded creativity outcomes.
notes: Both arms use GPT-4, with personalized tutor Mr. Ranedeer as treatment and standard ChatGPT-4 as control; the comparison is ai_design. The free-chat interaction and content supplied in Fig. 1 support open_chat rather than coach, and product-improvement ideas support task type idea_generation. The raters are trained, with no stated domain expertise, so the measure is human_raters. No outcome is named primary and no overall creativity score is reported; codebook Section 8 would choose originality (novelty rated by people) as the primary with_ai record. Self-efficacy is a pre-task self-report and eye tracking measures attention, so neither is listed as an output-scored creativity outcome; Table 2 gives correlations, not additional AI-condition contrasts. The three contrast reported fields retain exactly the c041 means, SDs, p-values and r values verified on PDF p. 8, Sect. 4.1. Related c246 Table 2 (PDF p. 11) has the same means, SDs and p-values but reports quality z = -3.24, r = -0.41; elaboration z = -6.25, r = -0.79; originality z = -1.65, r = -0.21, and confidence intervals for these r values. These journal statistics are separately attributed evidence, not replacements for c041's r = .42, .62 and .18. The signs of the journal Wilcoxon statistics should not override the direction evident in the arm means. No effect size or standard error has been computed; neither a z statistic alone nor an unexplained conflicting r settles the participant-level paired standard error required for pooling. The journal report supplies direct sequence-randomization evidence and product mapping for the matching sample; sharing a sample does not turn the experiment into an observational study. The linkage is inferred from the matching methods and exact results, not from an explicit cross-reference between papers. The original reconciliation object is retained unchanged as requested; its earlier uncertainty about randomization and sample overlap is superseded by this final review, the revised fields and final.open_items. Both markdown conversions were read in full, including c246's Appendix. Eligibility and all retained numerical results were checked against PDF text; the allocation diagrams and c041 Figs. 1 and 4 were also visually checked.

differences.resolved: open_chat, as in A. In both arms participants chatted freely with a GPT-4 chatbot through the OpenAI web interface. The codebook's coach code requires an AI that supplies no content, but Fig. 1 shows the personalized tutor proposing content in its third stage, and B's own how_used says both arms could supply content. The reconciled c132 and c141 (S2), whose AI arms chat freely with a chatbot and differ in another feature, also use open_chat. how_used records the tutor's Socratic questioning, which is the feature the ai_design contrast tests.
differences.quote: both built on OpenAI’s GPT-4 model and capable of responding to student prompts in natural language [...] Excellent! Let’s refine the idea using dynamic behavior learning and adaptive feedback loops...
differences.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 380): Sect. 3.2.1 (first part) and Fig. 1, personalized condition, stage 3 (second part)

differences.resolved: idea_generation, as in B. The paper cites the Torrance Product Improvement Task, but the version it used asks for three solutions to improve a product, as original and useful as possible, and raters scored quality, elaboration, and originality. The codebook puts product ideas under idea_generation. The reconciled c123 (Urban et al. 2024) uses the same three-solution, stuffed-bunny format with the same three rated dimensions and is coded idea_generation. c001, whose Torrance prompts asked participants to list as many ideas as possible, is coded divergent_test. The notes keep divergent_test as the alternative.
differences.quote: participants were asked to propose three solutions as original and useful as possible for two common products (e.g., a stuffed bunny and a portable coffee machine) using the assigned GAI tool.

differences.resolved: ['arm_means_sds_ns', 'standardized_effect', 'p_value_only'] on all three contrasts. Sect. 4.1 prints each arm's mean and SD, the Wilcoxon p-value, and r, with no Z, standard error, or confidence interval, so p_value_only applies beside the other codes, as in the reconciled c002 and c003. figure_only, listed in both forms, is dropped because Fig. 4A plots the same means and SDs that the text prints, as reconcilers ruled in c005 and c016. The n of 62 per arm comes from the within-subject design (Abstract, Sect. 3.1), not from the results.

Confirmed that c246 reports different z/r values, and added the separately attributed discrepancy to notes and open_questions. Neither source says that the journal values correct the chapter; the source does not justify silently replacing c041's values or deriving a participant-level paired standard error from the journal z values. The unresolved calculation issue affects extraction, not eligibility.
challenge_resolution.locator: c041 PDF p. 8 (printed p. 383), Sect. 4.1, elaboration and originality sentences. Compare c246 PDF p. 11 (printed p. 175), Results and Table 2: elaboration z = -6.25, r = -0.79; originality z = -1.65, r = -0.21.

open_items.item: Original question 1, condition-order randomization: resolved for screening by the matching-sample c246 Fig. 3 (PDF p. 9), which explicitly states random assignment. This previously affected criterion 1; no eligibility uncertainty remains on the combined source evidence.

Original question 2, product-to-task mapping: resolved by c246 Procedure (PDF p. 8) and Fig. 3 (p. 9). PIT 1 is the stuffed bunny and PIT 2 the portable coffee maker; both sequences complete the same product order with reversed AI order, so each product occurs under each AI configuration. No eligibility criterion remains unsettled.

Original question 3, aggregation of the three solutions into each participant's creativity score: still unspecified in both reports. Author clarification of scoring and the analysis unit would settle extraction/precision; it does not change the randomized design, 62-person sample, or output scoring.

Original question 4 and reconciliation.differences unresolved sample_overlap item: resolved for deduplication by comparing the retrieved c246 journal report with c041. Matching sample details, procedures and exact creativity results support treating these as one sample; neither report explicitly cross-identifies the other. Record one shared sample_id and one primary effect per sample/question/comparison. This does not reduce the sample below 50 or leave an eligibility criterion unsettled.

Original question 5, originality r/p consistency, expanded to the between-report elaboration and quality r discrepancies: c246 Table 2 supplies additional z/r/CI values but does not explicitly correct c041 or explain the differences. Authors' calculations and effect-size definition would settle which statistics to use for extraction and paired precision. The three eligibility criteria do not depend on the magnitude or significance of these effects.

Original question 6, Fig. 4B error bars: the c041 caption says SD, while the self-efficacy bars look inconsistent with the SDs printed in Sect. 4.1. Authors would need to identify the plotted uncertainty. This concerns an excluded self-report outcome and affects no eligibility criterion.
